It's October 2030. Lena has rented the shop next door. The café is almost ready. Only the name is missing. Lena, Andrei and Mara are sitting among boxes and paint pots.

Can I suggest something? Your bread recipe isn't only yours, but also your grandmother's. The bakery already has “Grandma Ingrid's recipes”. Why don't you simply call the café “Bei Ingrid”?
“Bei Ingrid”… Every Sunday Grandma used to invite the whole family round for cake. Everyone used to say: we're going to Ingrid's. At Ingrid's there's always coffee.
That's it. It's both warm and honest. And Ludwig won't think we're making fun of him. He'll cry.

“ent-VAY-der … OH-der”: stress on the second syllable.
Expresses a choice between two options. “Entweder” can stand in position 1 (with the verb after it or with normal word order) or in the middle; “oder” doesn't change the word order:
Either we find a name, or I'll call it “Café Brandt”.
We'll call it either “Bei Ingrid” or “Café Kastanie”.
Negates both elements. You DON'T add “nicht” or “kein”:
Wrong: “Ich trinke weder keinen Kaffee noch keinen Tee.” “weder … noch” already contains the negation (just like “neither… nor” in English).
3. Sowohl … als auch / nicht nur … sondern auch
Es gibt sowohl Kuchen als auch Suppe.
not only… but also (the second is surprising / more important)
Sie ist nicht nur Bäckerin, sondern auch Unternehmerin.
With “sowohl … als auch” as the subject, the verb is plural: “Sowohl die Gäste als auch Opa würden es lieben.”
“zwar” acknowledges a fact; “aber” brings in the objection. “Zwar” usually comes after the verb (or in position 1, with inversion):
The name is correct, admittedly, but it's boring.
In argumentation (B1 exams), “zwar … aber” is very useful: it shows you can see both sides. “Das Leben in der Stadt ist zwar teuer, aber es gibt viele Möglichkeiten.”
Either we find a name, or…
Both the customers and Grandpa would love it.

The café opened on a Saturday in November, exactly four years after Mara had first rung Ludwig's doorbell. Lena had been renovating for two months, both in the evenings after work and on every free Sunday. Andrei had painted the walls, Jakob had built shelves, Piotr had sanded the old floorboards until they shone like honey, and Kuba and Ola had painted the menu, with coloured pencils, with a little yellow tram in every corner.

The café was admittedly small, just three tables by the window and a long bench along the wall, but it was so welcoming that the first customers in the morning didn't want to leave. Old photographs of Kastanienallee hung on the walls: the street in 1905, when the house was built; tram line 46 in 1970, with a young tram driver with long hair; an inner courtyard full of people under a small chestnut tree, in 1974, at a wedding.

The new sign hung above the door. Andrei had painted it, in large, warm, curly letters, dark red on light wood: “Bei Ingrid”. Underneath, smaller: “Coffee, cake and time. Since 2030.” Nobody had told Ludwig what the café was going to be called. Lena wanted him to see for himself.

At seven o'clock, Ludwig came down, as he did every morning, with Fritz, to get his two bread rolls. He was now eighty-two and walked more slowly than before, with a walking stick that he neither liked nor wanted to admit he needed. He stopped in front of the bakery and looked to the left, at the new door, at the new sign.

He stood there for a long time. Fritz was pulling at the lead, because he could smell the rolls, but Ludwig didn't move. Lena came out of the bakery, in her white apron, and stood next to him. She said nothing. She waited.

Bei Ingrid. That's what she always used to say. Come over to mine, all of you. At my place there's always coffee. She didn't only cook for the family, but also for anyone who rang the doorbell. Colleagues, neighbours, strangers.
I know, Grandpa. That's why. So that there's a place like that again. Do you like it?

Ludwig didn't answer straight away. He took off his glasses and wiped them, for a very long time, with his handkerchief. Then he put them back on, opened the café door and went in. He sat down at the table by the window, from where you could see his M1 stop, and said: “A coffee, please. And a piece of plum cake. I'm the first customer.” And then, more quietly: “The dust, Lena. There's still a lot of dust in here from the renovation.” Lena nodded, just as seriously, and brought him his coffee.

Then Lena sat down next to him, just for a moment, even though the bakery next door was full and Emre was alone behind the counter. Ludwig told her about the Sundays at Ingrid's, which Lena had experienced as a little girl but could barely remember. How Ingrid laid the table every Sunday at three, with the white tablecloth and the cups with blue flowers. How she never knew how many people would come and so always baked two cakes, one for the family and one for everyone else. How colleagues from the trams came, neighbours, once even a young soldier from Russia who had got lost and didn't speak a word of German. Ingrid had given him coffee and cake and said: whoever rings my doorbell doesn't leave hungry. “That was her only law,” said Ludwig. “She had neither money nor time, but she always had a second cake.” Lena listened and secretly wrote a sentence on a napkin. The next day it hung, framed, above the counter: “Whoever rings our doorbell doesn't leave hungry. — Ingrid Brandt, 1950–2021.”

People came all day. Both the old neighbours and new faces from the neighbourhood. Mr Schulz, the Berlin patient, who was now eighty-six and still spoke nothing but Berlin dialect, came with his daughter and said: “I've heard this is the best cake in the whole of Berlin.” Dr Yılmaz came with her guitar. Mr Wolff came in uniform. The trader from the flea market, the one with the grey beard, came and brought an old coffee grinder as a present, “from the East, 1965, still works”.

Kuba and Ola had volunteered as waiters, in white aprons that reached down to their ankles. Kuba took the orders and wrote them in his school exercise book, with great concentration and lots of spelling mistakes. Ola carried the plates as carefully as if they were made of glass. When a customer asked if there was either tea or coffee, Kuba replied proudly: “Both! And cocoa. And water for dogs.” Bruno sat under the table by the window, next to Fritz, waiting for crumbs. He didn't have to wait long. By the end of the day, the two children had been given fourteen euros in tips. Kuba wanted to spend it straight away on dog food. Ola wanted to save it. They agreed on a compromise: neither one nor the other, but two pieces of cake for Ludwig and Mrs Hoffmann.

In the afternoon, Mrs Hoffmann was carried down the stairs by Jakob and Andrei, on her chair, like a queen. She was now ninety-four and said she liked neither stairs nor wheelchairs, but that she wouldn't miss this opening for anything in the world. Friedrich had come from Lübeck, together with Sophie. The two of them sat at the second table, hand in hand, and ordered coffee and two pieces of cheesecake. When Lena brought the cake, Friedrich said: “Either this is the best cheesecake in Germany, or I'm too happy to judge it.”

In the evening, when the last light was burning in the café and only the family was left, Jakob picked up his cello and Ludwig his guitar, and Mrs Hoffmann sat down at the old piano, which Piotr had brought down specially from Ludwig's flat. Friedrich picked up his violin. They played together, four instruments, four generations, in a small café on Kastanienallee that bore the name of a woman who was no longer there and yet was everywhere.

Mara stood at the door and watched. Andrei was standing next to her and put his arm around her shoulders. “Do you know what the best thing is?” he whispered. “We're not only customers here, but also family.” Mara nodded. Outside, the first snow of winter was falling on the new sign, on the letters, on the name. Bei Ingrid. And inside there was coffee. Always.
And, as Ingrid would have wanted, always a second cake too.
For anyone who rang the doorbell. For strangers too. Especially for strangers.
